claim: The European Commission's own decision quantifies the €500 million Apple DMA fine as approximately 0.14% of Apple's FY2024 annual worldwide turnover (USD 391,035,000,000 / ~EUR 360,729,787,500), the exact turnover figure sourced directly from Apple's 10-K.
stance_target: quantifying regulatory earnings exposure as a fraction of Apple's total revenue
scope_conditions: Apple FY2024 (ended 28 Sept 2024), Commission decision dated 23 April 2025
quoted_support: This amount is proportionate, as it represents a relatively small proportion of Apple's annual worldwide turnover (approx.0.14 %) and in any event significantly less than the maximum fine cap of 10 % referred to in the previous recital.

claim: Apple's Article 5(4) DMA non-compliance is legally established as continuous and ongoing from 7 March 2024 through at least the date of the decision (23 April 2025) — over 13 months of violation — with the Commission treating first-decision status as a mitigating factor that would not apply to future violations.
stance_target: duration and recurrence risk of Apple's DMA regulatory exposure over a 2-5 year holding horizon
scope_conditions: EU App Store, Art. 5(4) DMA, 7 March 2024 onward
quoted_support: Apple Inc. has not complied with Article 5(4) of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925 from 7 March 2024 and such non-compliance is on-going... the Commission has taken into account the mitigating circumstance that this Decision is among the very first non-compliance decisions adopted under Regulation (EU) 2022/1925.

claim: The Commission found Apple's App Store had on average over 130 million recipients (users) in the EU during the relevant period, per Apple's own DSA Transparency Report, establishing the scale of the EU user base subject to the anti-steering restrictions.
stance_target: scale of EU installed base exposed to steering restrictions/App Store economics
scope_conditions: EU App Store users, per Apple's Digital Services Act Transparency Report, relevant period pre-2025
quoted_support: the App Store had on average over 130 million recipients in the Union during the relevant period.
numbers: 130 million average EU App Store recipients

claim: The Commission rejected Apple's argument that Article 5(4) DMA was too novel and legally uncertain to support a finding of serious non-compliance, holding instead that Apple 'could not have been unaware' its business terms could breach the DMA.
stance_target: Apple's legal defense that DMA obligations were insufficiently crystallized to justify serious sanctions
quoted_support: It follows that Apple could not have been unaware that the maintenance of the three Business Terms described in this Decision, as well as the rules set out in these business terms respectively, could lead to a breach of Article 5(4) of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925.

claim: Beyond the one-time €500M fine, Apple faces recurring periodic penalty payments (up to the Article 31(1) statutory limit of 5% of average daily worldwide turnover) for every day of continued non-compliance if it fails to remedy the Art. 5(4) breach within 60 days of notification — a distinct, escalating, ongoing category of regulatory earnings exposure beyond the settled fine.
stance_target: regulatory exposure to Apple's earnings is a recurring risk, not a one-time settled cost, over a multi-year holding horizon
scope_conditions: EU DMA Article 31(1), effective from 60 days post-notification of the 23 April 2025 decision
quoted_support: If the addressee of this Decision fails to comply with Article 3 within 60 calendar days from the date of notification of this Decision, it shall incur periodic penalty payments not exceeding the limit stipulated in Article 31(1) of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925, from the date on which it is required to bring the non-compliance effectively to an end pursuant to Article 3, until the date on which it complies with the Decision.
numbers: up to 5% of average daily worldwide turnover per day (per Art. 31(1), cited in companion sources)

claim: The Commission's required remedies mandate that any Apple fee for facilitating initial user acquisition via the App Store must be tied only to that initial acquisition in time and scope, commensurate to its value net of other remuneration, and must not 'remunerate the gatekeeper for gatekeeper value' — directly constraining Apple's ability to design a fee structure that recovers ongoing platform value from steered/off-platform transactions.
stance_target: Apple can preserve most App Store commission economics simply by relabeling fees after the steering ruling
scope_conditions: EU App Store, remediation under Art. 3 of the DMA.100109 decision
quoted_support: is commensurate to the value of the initial acquisition and must take into account any other, direct or indirect, remuneration received from business users for facilitating the initial acquisition; and; (iii) does not remunerate the gatekeeper for gatekeeper value.
